What are must know life hacks when going on a road trip? Cross country or cross town?

Don't bring a child (or adult) who will ask "Are we there yet??" every five seconds.

That's all I got so far. I'll let you know if I come up with more.
That will never be a problem. Childfree is the way to be! (For me)
Be sure to have paper maps/an atlas in the vehicle. It's amazing these days how many people travel unknown roads without this resource, relying solely on electronic devices.

My girlfriend and I took a couple cross country road trips over the past few years and we only navigate with a road atlas. It is honestly so much more fun than just typing it into your phone GPS. We used our phones for small things like exact addresses but an atlas is the way to go for the general driving.

I love using them too. If you really want to go all out get the Rand McNally spiral bound atlas with the laminated pages. That way you can use dry erase markers and plot your entire trip right on the maps. It lets you easily visualize the whole route and check ahead for things like construction, etc.

Also, usually the road atlases have time zone maps. These can really help you out in areas where the zones are drawn in a weird way.
That's exactly the one I have! It is amazing! My aunt got it for me as a silly little gift but it has honestly been one of my favorite presents.
Find costcos along the way for cheap eats, awesome supplies, and gas!
How big of a car are you driving that you can get supplies at Costco for a road trip, need a roll of paper towels? how about 50 rolls.

Water bottles are great in bulk. Or a bag/box of snacks. You'd be surprised how quickly a family of four can go through trail mix or a bag of oranges from costco. Supplies can be more then just paper towels.
A lot of the gas stations that are right off the freeway tend to be more expensive. Go into town a few blocks and you'll see it drop a few pennies.
Make sure you are driving a luxurious American made vehicle, and if you're like me, make sure you put the top down

In this day and age, always pre-load the maps that you're going to use on your trip. It's always good to have both offline maps on your phone and old fashioned paper maps. Even with today's modern technology, GPS signals still have yet to be 100% reliable.

Another tip is to bring snacks and drinks with you in a cooler full of ice. It'll not only save you money, but if you're traveling with kids (and even adults) they'll get hungry and snacks will hold them over until you can find a nice restaurant to stop at along your trip.

If it's possible, and you can adjust your sleep cycle, summer road trips are much easier for me when I'm driving at night. Not only are the roads more empty, but the cooler night time temp helps make the trip more enjoyable.

Pick up hitch hikers if you have space in your car. Hitchers are usually full of great stories and rarely out to murder you.

Also, just try not to say no. If you stop for gas and someone suggests something cool down the road, go there, even if it is off your path. Often the greatest parts of an adventure are the least expected.

Don't gas up in the middle of the day, do it first thing in the morning or at night. I've always been told to do this you get more gas. Something about the heat of the day and the volume dispensed being off at the pump because gas expands.

Tips from a former long haul truck driver:

-bring extra bottled water and snacks like protein bars (my favorite is walmart brand almond $2.50 a box and lowest carb bars out there)

-leave an extra empty bottle or two for emergencies (you might get stuck in traffic or somewhere you can't pull over)

-load up on free audiobooks and podcasts

-get a Rand McNally road atlas, it will save your ass if your phone goes out

-get a good night sleep, if you feel sleepy pull over and close your eyes for 10 mins, even if you don't sleep it will help

-bring a can of moist towelettes and a roll of paper towels, you can clean yourself much better in rest areas and truck stops with these- you need something sturdy like a paper towel after you use a moist towelette, and many road bathrooms have super thin paper that will break apart (trust me on this)

-if you're doing frequent long road trips, get satellite radio, howard stern can fill half a day easy

-remember, two digit interstates ending in an odd number run north/south, even (including zero) run east/west

-if you need a free shower for whatever reason, stop at a truck stop and ask a trucker going in to the store - chances are they have free showers on their rewards card and will give you one if you ask nicely (it cost average $12 per shower at most truck stops)

-when you eat meals, eat light and snack along the way, if you eat a big meal you'll get sleepy

-alcohol the night before a trip will make you much more tired the next day, even 1 drink

-if you travel all the time, definitely get a CB Radio and good antenna - it's fun talking to truckers and they will advise you of accidents/construction and give you the right exit number to turn off

Wow! Some awesome advice! I never thought of the moist towelettes. I usually suck it up until my destination. But the longest I've ever gone is like 20 hours so it isn't terrible.

Do your feet ever swell from sitting so long? Cruise control has saved my life though, well my legs.

yeah that was a huge issue for me as a beginning truck driver - i hated using public toilets...still do

no i never had any problems with feet swelling, but my back used to hurt every now and then
I was just gonna mention the empty bottle and wipes. This is an awesome reply.

Pack your own food.

You don't have to stop every few hours for a meal. You're not victim to fast food restaurants. And you can eat what you like.

Find a local grocery store, stock up on sandwich, salad, and snack foods. Prepare before leaving in the morning from your hotel room or whatever, and you won't be shackled to a town or a route that has prepared food waiting for consumers. Freedom!
True. The fast food makes me feel like shit.

Try to keep driving under 10 hours a day. Once that 10 hour mark hits, every minute afterward feels like an hour.

Also http://www.roadsideamerica.com/ is an awesome site to find stops along the way

Podcasts and audiobooks! Lots and lots of those.

Also, ritalin/adderal if you've the means.
Do you think meth is a good substitute? ;-) it's pretty cheap.
I mean I'd recommend moderation is all
Planet Fitness Black Card membership. Access to climate-controlled gym and showers near most places in the US for $20 a month.

Unless you are completely desperate and there are no other available options, skip fast food and chain restaurants. Go for diners, independently run restaurants, ask locals for suggestions. There's no point in traveling if you're going to stick to the same generic formulaic crap you can find anywhere in the US. Try stuff that is truly representative of where you're passing through.
Yeah, when I'm in a time crunch I always do fast food cause of the drive through. I am a big fan on Zaxby's. I feel like it's Chickfila...without controversy and better tenders.

I have some experience travelling by car, camper and boat. My $0.02.

Carry tools and spare parts for your car. Make sure the spare tire is good and the tire iron and jack work. Learn to change the tire and boost the car. Keep emergency flares and reflective vest in the trunk. Have someone you trust look over the vehicle before you go.

My car kit includes, tools, spare belts, fuses, wipers, wiper fluid, flashlight, leatherman, batteries, emergency blanket, small empty gas can, tire repair and inflator, manual air pump for tires, rope, some food, fabric tape, small bottle of water, acetominaphin, topical antiseptic, antibiotics (cipro), flares, reflective triangle, reflective vest, rain coat, cb radio with magnetic antenna, booster cables, multimeter, some electrical connectors and tape, duct tape, thin metal wire, traction aids and a big lead pipe to help with leverage on stuck lug nuts.

Keep a small pairing knife, utensils, napkins, salt, sugar and creamer packets in the car because they F you in the drive through. Also, gel hand cleaner is very handy.

Cell phone coverage is not the same for the big networks. Try to get a cheap second phone on the competing net for emergencies. Some phones with unactivated sims will still work for 911 calls.

iPads have better cell reception than phones. I've used voip on an iPad in the desert where no phone could get a signal.

Audiobooks are your friend, as are crosswords and puzzles (being read by the passenger)

If you are using your phone for gps or entertainment, get a mount. Don't hold it in your hand. Might be illegal to hold a phone while driving and it is very distracting.

Plan you next day the night before, but don't feel limited to that plan. If you are travelling for pleasure, your planning is mostly to find the best attractions that you want to visit.

Atlases are great for planning even if you use a gps. Look at travel guides; some of the best spots are not well known. Ask locals.

Twitter is a pretty good way to get the feel for what is going on in the area as are local newspapers, especially the weeklies.

Keep hydrated and get rest. Eat well; try to avoid junk food as much as possible. Most grocery stores have ready meals, salad bars, and healthier options. Sunflower seeds are great for keeping your hands busy. If your electrolytes get low, you can pick up hydration packs at most pharmacies.

Watch your speed. Lots of towns and cities make their budget off of speeding tourists.

Baby wipes are great for keeping clean. So are quick dry clothes. Wash your socks and undies in the sink and let dry overnight.

Tell your bank and credit card company that you are travelling or you risk triggering their fraud protection systems and having your card put on hold. Make sure you know the contact details for your bank and cc companies, usually printed on the cards.

If you need something shipped, many places will only ship to the address on your credit card. You can call your bank and have a second address added if that is the case. Many UPS stores will accept shipments to hold for a day or two for you, but call them first.

Make sure your car and health insurance covers you out of state/country.

Get travel and accidental health insurance. Most of these are priced based on the cost of airline travel and packaged vacations, so you might get a good price.

Bring your medications and some spare in case the trip lasts longer. Nothing chews up a day and $ faster than trying to get meds away from home.

Some big box stores let you spend the night in their parking lot. There are apps to find which and you can always ask the manager. This is only for sleeping the in vehicle; no tents...

Emergency bowel movements can be handled by a sturdy bag with a handful of clumping cat litter. Triple the bag while using then properly dispose of the inner two. You can also get wag-bags at Walmart and camping supply stores.

Showers can be had at truck stops, YMCAs, and other sports clubs. Some clubs have a trial membership good for a few hours, so have a workout and a shower, then buy the staff coffees on your way out.

Don't use propane or butane heaters in the vehicles or tents unless you have excellent ventilation. The carbon monoxide is deadly. If you need to heat a van or tent, there are catalytic heaters available, just don't leave them unattended.

You get surprisingly better gas mileage from gas purchased in warm places. Winter formulated gas sucks.

Passport, do you have one? Is there a possibility you might need one?

Have someone check on your home while you are away. Many insurance companies require a visit at least every three days.

Many hotels/motels have cheaper prices online than if you walk in. Alway check. Also if you have any club or affiliations, mention them and you might get a discount. Be really nice to hotel staff, they can get you deals, and are there to look out for you while you are staying there. You want them on your side.

Trucks are your friends on highways. If they suddenly slow down, look out for speed traps and obstructions. Don't pass them on their right, they can see you. If you can't see their mirrors, they can't see you. If they want in to your lane, let them and signal by flashing your lights at them. If they flash their running lights, they are saying thanks.

If you see a sign for deer crossing, watch out for them. At night, you can often see their eyes reflecting your headlights. If you see one on the side of the road, watch out and maybe put your hazard lights on and slow down.

Have a great trip.
First thing came into my mind: if she says she has to pee, that's what she means. No delays, get on it.

Trucks are your friends on highways. If they suddenly slow down, look out for speed traps and obstructions. Don't pass them on their right, they can see you. Have a great trip.

My car kit includes, tools, spare belts, fuses, wipers, wiper fluid, flashlight, leatherman, batteries, emergency blanket, small empty gas can, tire repair and inflator, manual air pump for tires, rope, some food, fabric tape, small bottle of water, acetominaphin, topical antiseptic, antibiotics (cipro), flares, reflective triangle, reflective vest, rain coat, cb radio with magnetic antenna, booster cables, multimeter, some electrical connectors and tape, duct tape, thin metal wire, traction aids and a big lead pipe to help with leverage on stuck lug nuts.

Keep a small pairing knife, utensils, napkins, salt, sugar and creamer packets in the car because they F you in the drive through. Also, gel hand cleaner is very handy.

iPads have better cell reception than phones. I've used voip on an iPad in the desert where no phone could get a signal.

Audiobooks are your friend, as are crosswords and puzzles (being read by the passenger)

If you are using your phone for gps or entertainment, get a mount. Don't hold it in your hand. Might be illegal to hold a phone while driving and it is very distracting.

Plan you next day the night before, but don't feel limited to that plan. If you are travelling for pleasure, your planning is mostly to find the best attractions that you want to visit.

Atlases are great for planning even if you use a gps. Look at travel guides; some of the best spots are not well known. Ask locals.

Twitter is a pretty good way to get the feel for what is going on in the area as are local newspapers, especially the weeklies.

Watch your speed. Lots of towns and cities make their budget off of speeding tourists.

Baby wipes are great for keeping clean. So are quick dry clothes. Wash your socks and undies in the sink and let dry overnight.

Get travel and accidental health insurance. Most of these are priced based on the cost of airline travel and packaged vacations, so you might get a good price.

Bring your medications and some spare in case the trip lasts longer. Nothing chews up a day and $ faster than trying to get meds away from home.

We all know it was a huge deal back in middle/high school, college, etc. (based on your age) to have a great away message on AIM. Any great old messages floating in Voaters' memories?
Previous Users of AOL Instant Messenger (AIM), What Was Your Best Away Message?

Probably not my best, but the only one that I can remember explicitly was lyrics from a New Order song. "I've got to go home, I've been so alone you see." The girl that I loved said it was stupid and didn't make any sense. I was a pretty sad teen.
I think my husband's was "I'm probably pooping right now."

I suppose the best one I had is the only one that has a story with it.

9th grade: I went over to a girls house. We had been interested in each other, but had never spent time alone. We watched a movie and made-out a little bit. We never discussed dating or anything. After the movie, I went home and got on AIM as I usually would.

Immediately I have several conversation requests from people off my buddy list. I reluctantly accept them and it's some of the girl's friends that I'm merely acquaintances with. They were asking me a bunch of questions, probably out of loyalty to the girl, but also out of curiosity. They all know what has happened. I'm getting swamped with messages from them, but then my Mom called upstairs demanding help in the garage. I quickly set my away message go to help.

At the time, I had a tool that caused my away message to be a random line from the lyrics of the current song in my media player. Coincidentally, the song that was playing when I went away had a lyric in it like, I'm never going do that again... and that's what got sent out to all of this girl's friends, right in the middle of them asking me about my intentions with her.

When I finally return to my computer, I'm greeted with dozens of messages telling me what an asshole I am. Not only that, but her friends had informed her of my message to which she became "devastated" and started crying. I felt terrible.

I was able to talk to her about it and I showed her the lyric-away-message tool. It took a bit of time but she accepted my apologies and understood the accident. We never spent time alone after that though. A little while later she started dating a different guy who was a better fit anyways, so it all worked out in the end.

The crazy thing is, she wasn't a very good kisser and so I was on the fence about pursuing things with her further. That said, I was in 9th grade, so saying I would "never do it again"... ha!

I always used lyrics from wannabe pop bands based on how I felt about my current relationship. I don't know what I was thinking.

I tried to be funny once and put "is typing..." but then my ex freaked out and asked why I didn't send anything for two hours.

The writer require lesson in English.

Typically when I play Dota, I put myself in the support role for a couple of reasons:

  1. People usually never support unless I'm in a five stack, then I can pander around with some heroes.

  2. ^ Similar to the above, I never really had much opportunity to play anything other than support (but I do play some DP and Necrophos occasionally)

  3. I feel like there is less pressure to "perform."

Now, that being said, I have 2 main heroes who I love to go support as, as a single support. Shadow Demon and Crystal Maiden. Shadow Demon is my main support hero considering that all he really needs is boots, and he's golden. Anything else is luxury. Same with Crystal Maiden. This frees me up to buy wards, dust, or whatever else people need without worrying about getting x, y, z item to fulfill my kit and thus be more useful.

I have more trouble with Crystal Maiden because she's very squishy, harder to farm with, and she's inevitably, very, very slow.

So this leads me to wanting to change things up a bit in who I support with. I have branched out to Pugna and Vengeful Spirit, however, I feel that they need a bit of item usage to be terribly useful? Perhaps I am incorrect in that assumption. But with Pugna and Venge, I have more utility in assisting with kills and team fight power.

Voat, what are your thoughts?

Edit: Formatting. Less Eye Bleeding.

I used to always pick Disruptor as position 5 cause all I used to need was brown boots (maybe arcanes) and force staff and that was it. Especially because his abilities are so damn good if you're playing with a couple other people too
Winter Wyvern is amazing right now. It keeps your idiots alive. She is anti-aggression. Easy to play.

Also has a bit of potential to screw your team mates over a bit as well though with 'freezing' them in place, so she's kind of relient on decision making. I've definitely seen opponents using her healing in lane as a way to engage (just worth bearing in mind).

true. one way to avoid this is not use it in a team fight, you lose some potential but at least you'll always use it right. I use it only when I know we are alone or the enemy is just right clickers. Other than the, she is fairly easy to use and i tend to use her ult as a disable.

If you're going to use it in a team fight, the other rule can be to make sure you're using it on people that are being focused or people that are stunned (as if they're stunned, they wouldn't be able to do anything anyway).

I probably wouldn't use Pugna as a support. Like you said, he's pretty item dependant and doesn't offer huge amounts of utility (he has no stuns and if you're the only support, you probably want to pick one with at least a bit of crowd control).

Treant Protector is someone you could definitely look into trying as a hard support. He works great with just boots. Offers a global heal that can also be used on towers. He can go invis to place wards and scout the map. He can give initiation with his ult if your team needs it. His Agh's upgrade is amazing if you somehow manage to find farm (it will basically give you global vision and allow you to ult from across the map with proper preparation). His right click damage is pretty big at the start of the game and that can help you zone pretty easily.

Others to have a look at might be Shadow Shaman, Lich, Bane, Witch Doctor and Earthshaker; though I think they're more general supports, where Treant can be a great hard 5.

I love e treant to pieces! He's one of my favorites even before he got the ages upgrade. I find him so much easier to play now than he was before his... Buff?

I typically play him pretty passively by farming jungle and healing my carries. Works well fifty percent of the time. If there's a Phoenix, or a husker on the team I find he pairs well with them because their abilities harm themselves. I can just heal them and they can keep bashing.
